Article https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76506-3 Allele-speciﬁc chromatin architecture shapes imprinted domains and coordinates a distal enhancer and antisense transcription at the mouse Mest-Copg2 domain

Bongmin Bae , Katherine Gu , Daniel Loftus & Amanda J. Whipple

Genomic imprinting results in parent-of-origin-dependent gene expression, but how three-dimensional genome organization contributes to imprinted gene regulation remains unclear. Using Capture Hi-C in mouse cortex and primary cortical neurons, we identiﬁed parental allele-speciﬁc chromatin architectures across multiple imprinted domains. These architectures largely originate from imprinting control regions and correlate with DNA methylationsensitive CTCF binding. Active and inactive alleles of imprinted genes show distinct promoter interaction proﬁles and differential engagement with distal regulatory elements in both contact frequency and the epigenetic state of distal regions. A CRISPR interference screen identiﬁed a distal enhancer that regulates Mest-Copg2 imprinted expression through allele-speciﬁc chromatin interactions. In neurons, this enhancer activates Copg2 on the maternal allele, whereas on the paternal allele it drives Mest isoforms transcribed antisense to Copg2 and contributes to Copg2 repression. In summary, we show that allelespeciﬁc chromatin architecture coordinates maternal enhancer activity and paternal antisense transcription to control imprinted expression in neurons.

Three-dimensional (3D) genome organization in the nucleus spans multiple hierarchical scales and has been widely implicated in gene regulation1,2. At the compartment level, chromatin is partitioned into A and B compartments, which largely correspond to transcriptionally active and inactive regions, respectively3. At a ﬁner scale, chromatin is organized into topologically associating domains (TADs)4,5, within which gene regulatory mechanisms, such as chromatin loop-mediated enhancer-promoter communication, take place6–8. TADs also serve to insulate regulatory effects between neighboring domains9,10, although recent evidence suggests that some regulatory crosstalk can occur across TAD boundaries11. Allele-speciﬁc chromatin architectures have been identiﬁed in both genome-wide Hi-C studies in mouse and human cells7,12,13 and in locus-speciﬁc studies at imprinted domains14–18, revealing parent-of-origin-speciﬁc chromatin organization. Since genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon where gene

expression is restricted to or biased toward a single parental allele, these observations provide a strong rationale for further dissecting the contribution of chromatin architecture to the regulation of imprinted expression. Imprinting control regions (ICRs), which correspond to germlineestablished differentially methylated regions (gDMRs), are key regulatory elements that orchestrate imprinted gene expression across long genomic distances and are deﬁned by parent-of-origin-speciﬁc CpG methylation that is maintained throughout development19–22. These primary imprinting marks direct the establishment of secondary, somatic differentially methylated regions (sDMRs) at a subset of gene promoters during development20,23. Promoter-associated DMRs can directly regulate transcription by modulating access to regulatory sequences, thereby restricting expression to the unmethylated parental allele. DMRs, indicating that ICRs can also exert control through long-range regulatory mechanisms. Two major mechanisms have been described for long-range regulation of imprinted genes: cis-acting long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) and higher-order chromatin architecture. At many loci, unmethylated ICRs drive transcription of lncRNAs that act in cis to repress neighboring imprinted genes. For instance, Snhg14 lncRNA transcriptionally silences paternal Ube3a expression in neurons24,25, whereas Kcnq1ot1 lncRNA recruits and spreads repressive chromatin modiﬁers across neighboring genes26–28. At other loci, ICRs can regulate distal genes by organizing higher-order chromatin architecture through methylationsensitive binding of the CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF), a key mediator of chromatin looping29. This mechanism was ﬁrst characterized at the H19-Igf2 locus, where CTCF binding at the unmethylated ICR insulates the maternal Igf2 promoter from its distal enhancer, restricting expression to the paternal allele14,30,31. More recently, additional locusspeciﬁc studies have shown that allele-speciﬁc chromatin interactions between enhancers and promoters are a central mechanism of imprinted expression14–18. Together, these studies suggest that imprinted expression can be regulated through both transcriptional and architectural mechanisms. However, a systematic examination of allele-speciﬁc chromatin architecture across imprinted domains is still lacking. Although recent technical advances have revealed allelic biases at sub-TAD scales, few studies have functionally linked these structures to imprinted expression. Moreover, how transcriptional repression by lncRNAs and chromatin insulation mechanisms act together to establish or maintain imprinted expression remains unclear. In this work, we generated high-resolution, allele-speciﬁc chromatin contact maps across multiple imprinted domains in the mouse brain, enabling systematic analysis of how DNA methylation at DMRs inﬂuences chromatin insulation and providing evidence for longdistance regulation. To identify functional cis-regulatory elements, we performed CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) screens and identiﬁed a distal enhancer at the Mest-Copg2 domain whose activity is correlated with allele-speciﬁc chromatin interactions. We further show that Copg2 imprinted expression in neurons is regulated by both enhancer activity and antisense transcription, with the enhancer directly promoting maternal Copg2 through allele-speciﬁc chromatin interactions, while the nuclear-enriched antisense transcript MestXL selectively represses paternal Copg2. Together, these ﬁndings underscore the critical role of 3D genome folding in coordinating enhancer function and transcriptional repression at imprinted loci.

Results Imprinted domains exhibit allele-speciﬁc chromatin architectures Given the characteristic monoallelic expression pattern of imprinted genes, we asked whether imprinted domains exhibit allele-speciﬁc chromatin organization. A recent study suggested the presence of such structures at a subset of imprinted domains in the mouse brain13. To systematically examine the relationship between allelic chromatin architecture and imprinted expression at higher resolution, we performed region Capture Hi-C on cortical tissue from reciprocal F1 hybrid mice (BL6 x CAST and CAST x BL6; two biological replicates per cross). Capture probes targeted ~23 Mb spanning eight imprinted domains, and libraries were sequenced to high depth (Supplementary Fig. 1a). After applying HICUP quality control for mapping, ligation, and PCR duplication, 10 to 17 million valid paired reads were obtained per sample (5–9% of total sequenced reads). Consistent with the spatial segregation of chromosomes, interchromosomal (trans) interactions occur at a lower frequency than intrachromosomal (cis) interactions (Supplementary Fig. 1a). Sequencing reads were phased by parental origin using strain-speciﬁc single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Approximately 25% of valid reads were allelically informative,

reﬂecting the fraction of both ends of reads overlapping strain-speciﬁc SNPs (Supplementary Fig. 1b). Using the cis-allelic read pairs, we generated allele-speciﬁc Hi-C contact matrices at up to 5 kb resolution (Supplementary Fig. 1c). To control for differences in allelic coverage and strain-of-origin effects, reads from reciprocal crosses were downsampled to equal depth and combined by parent-of-origin prior to analysis. Across the eight imprinted domains examined (Peg10-Sgce, Mest-Copg2, Peg3-Usp29, Snrpn-Peg12, H19-Igf2, Kcnq1-Kcnq1ot1, Meg3-Dio3, and Peg13-Kcnk9), most domains exhibited clear allele-speciﬁc chromatin architectures, although the magnitude of these differences varied between loci (Fig. 1a–p, and Supplementary Figs. 2–9). Importantly, the interaction patterns were highly consistent between reciprocal crosses, indicating that the observed differences reﬂect parent-of-origin effects rather than strain-speciﬁc differences (Supplementary Fig. 10). Allele-speciﬁc chromatin features observed by Capture Hi-C included distinct TAD-like structures, prominent chromatin loops between distal loci, and architectural stripes consistent with slow loop extrusion (Fig. 1a–h). Differences in chromatin architectures between the two parental alleles can be further visualized as allelic subtraction maps and loops speciﬁc to each parental allele (Fig. 1i–p). Collectively, these results revealed widespread allele-speciﬁc chromatin organization across imprinted domains in the mouse brain.

Methylation-sensitive CTCF at ICRs shapes allelic architecture Given the central role of ICRs in regulating imprinted gene expression, we asked whether allele-speciﬁc chromatin architectures are anchored at ICRs and associated DMRs. Allele-speciﬁc DMRs, including both gDMRs and sDMRs, have been previously identiﬁed in the mouse brain32. To assess their relationship with chromatin organization, we performed pile-up contact analysis using our Capture Hi-C data, quantifying chromatin interactions within a 150 kb window centered on each DMR (Supplementary Fig. 11a). Pile-up analysis across all gDMRs (n = 8) revealed pronounced allele-speciﬁc differences in chromatin architecture. Methylated alleles at gDMRs displayed relatively uniform interaction patterns (insulation score = 0.90), whereas the unmethylated alleles exhibited strong local insulation (insulation score = 1.87), resulting in reduced interaction frequencies across the DMR (Fig. 2a). In contrast, pile-up analysis across sDMRs (n = 21) showed more modest allelic differences, with similar insulation scores between the methylated and unmethylated alleles at sDMRs (1.21 and 1.42, respectively; Fig. 2b). These results are consistent with a previously proposed model in which unmethylated alleles of ICRs act as chromatin insulators or domain boundaries that restrict interactions between adjacent regions9,14,15,17. To assess whether these insulation features are associated with CTCF binding, we performed CTCF CUT&Tag in hybrid primary cortical neurons. We observed strong allele-speciﬁc CTCF binding at imprinted domains, including 17 paternally biased and 4 maternally biased CTCF peaks (Fig. 2c). These peaks were detected within our Hi-C capture regions (Peg10-Sgce, Mest-Copg2, Peg3-Usp29, Snrpn-Peg12, H19-Igf2, Kcnq1-Kcnq1ot1, Meg3-Dio3, and Peg13-Kcnk9) and additional imprinted loci (H13, Gnas, Grb10, Commd1, and Impact), largely consistent with previous reports in mouse brain29. Notably, allele-speciﬁc CTCF binding was enriched at the unmethylated allele relative to the methylated allele at DMRs and coincided with regions of strong chromatin insulation (Fig. 2a,b). This enrichment was strongest at gDMRs but also observed at sDMRs, including the Meg3 promoter (Supplementary Fig. 11b). These results provide systematic support for a model in which DNA methylation-sensitive CTCF binding at ICRs contributes to allele-speciﬁc chromatin insulation across imprinted loci. Although DNMTi treatment was more toxic in NPCs, the limited demethylation and preserved imprinted expression likely reﬂect slower cell division rates and/or additional mechanisms that maintain imprinting in more differentiated cells. To identify additional epigenetic features associated with the allele-speciﬁc chromatin organization, we next analyzed histone modiﬁcation proﬁles (Fig. 2g). Active histone marks, including H3K27ac, H3K4me3, and H3K36me3, were preferentially enriched at the unmethylated allele at gDMRs, whereas the repressive histone mark H3K9me3 was associated with the methylated allele. H3K27me3 was also enriched at the unmethylated allele at gDMRs, consistent with its known mutual exclusivity with DNA methylation35. These patterns indicate that allele-speciﬁc chromatin architecture is accompanied by distinct local chromatin states at DMRs, consistent with previous observations36,37. Together with the observed CTCF-dependent insulation, these features support an established model in which DNA methylation and chromatin state jointly shape allele-speciﬁc

regulatory environments, which may inﬂuence interactions with distal regulatory elements.

Neural-speciﬁc chromatin organization at the Meg3 locus During our analysis of chromatin architecture in the cortex, we identiﬁed a region in which allele-speciﬁc chromatin organization was not directly associated with CTCF binding. At the Meg3-Dio3 imprinted domain, a 210 kb region spanning the Meg3 lncRNA gene body is largely devoid of long-range chromatin contacts on the maternal allele (Fig. 3a, grey highlight). The 5′ boundary of this region coincides with a strong maternal-speciﬁc CTCF peak, whereas no prominent CTCF binding is detected at the 3’ end. Although several imprinted lncRNAs, such as Airn and Kcnq1ot1, lead to deposition of H3K27me338, the Meg3 gene body did not show enrichment of this mark. Active and inactive alleles engage distinct regulatory landscapes Having established that imprinted domains exhibit distinct allelespeciﬁc chromatin architectures, we next investigated how these

structural differences relate to imprinted gene expression. Similar patterns were observed in primary cortical neurons (Supplementary Fig. 12b,c). To further characterize the regulatory potential of allele-speciﬁc chromatin interactions, we asked whether distal regions contacted by imprinted gene promoters differ in their chromatin states between alleles, particularly for non-DMR imprinted genes that show similar contact frequencies. To address this, we classiﬁed chromatin states across imprinted domains using ChromHMM40, integrating publicly available ChIP-seq data with our allelic CUT&Tag datasets from neuronal cells and tissue. The input features included allele-speciﬁc CTCF, H3K36me3, H3K27me3, H3K27ac and H3K4me3 proﬁles, as well as non-allelic H3K4me1 data. Chromatin states were deﬁned based on combinations of active and repressive histone marks and grouped into functional categories, including active enhancers, transcribed regions, repressive chromatin, and quiescent states (Fig. 4d). We then quantiﬁed the frequency of TSS-anchored contacts with ChromHMM-deﬁned chromatin states. Non-imprinted genes exhibited minimal allelic differences in contacts with regions annotated as active enhancers or repressive chromatin. In contrast, for non-DMR imprinted genes, the active allele preferentially contacted regions annotated as active enhancers compared to the inactive allele, in both cortex and primary cortical neurons (Fig. 4e, and Supplementary Fig. 12d). Together, these results indicate that allele-speciﬁc gene expression is associated with increased interaction frequency (or hubness) and, in some cases, preferential engagement with active regulatory elements.

CRISPRi screening reveals a distal enhancer for the Mest- Copg2 domain Our Capture Hi-C analysis provided chromatin interaction maps at 5 kb resolution; however, regulatory elements are often smaller than this scale. We therefore reﬁned candidate cis-regulatory regions using chromatin accessibility proﬁling. ATAC-seq on hybrid mouse cortex identiﬁed ~78,000 accessible regions genome-wide. Using allelespeciﬁc SNPs, we identiﬁed ~100 peaks with allele-speciﬁc accessibility, most of which overlapped known imprinted promoters or DMRs (Supplementary Fig. 13a). Only a small number of allele-speciﬁc peaks were detected outside these regions, suggesting that allele-speciﬁc accessibility of regulatory elements is relatively rare at this resolution. To identify functional cis-regulatory elements involved in imprinting, we performed a CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) screen using a nuclease-dead Cas9 (dCas9) fused to the KRAB repressor domain (Fig. 5a). To facilitate the assessment of imprinted expression in neurons, we established hybrid NPCs from dCas9-KRAB (BL6) x CAST F1 embryos, delivered guide RNAs (gRNAs) by lentiviral transduction, and differentiated the cells into neurons. NPC-derived neurons recapitulated allele-speciﬁc CTCF binding at ICRs (Supplementary Fig. 13b), consistent with primary neurons, indicating that this system preserves imprinted features. We focused on the Mest-Copg2 domain, which exhibits distinct patterns of allele-speciﬁc expression. Mest is exclusively expressed from the paternal allele across tissues. In contrast, Copg2 is biallelically expressed in most tissues but shows a maternal expression bias speciﬁcally in neurons, despite lacking a promoter-associated DMR, suggesting regulation beyond promoter-proximal methylation. We designed gRNAs targeting 25 accessible chromatin peaks within this domain (Fig. 5b, and Supplementary Table 1). Each region was targeted individually in NPCs, and expression of Mest and Copg2 expression was measured following neuronal differentiation (Fig. 5c). Among these candidates, inhibition of a single element (E105) signiﬁcantly reduced Mest expression, while total Copg2 levels were unchanged (Fig. 5c).

Given the maternal bias of Copg2 expression in neurons, we next assessed allele-speciﬁc expression using RT-digital droplet PCR (ddPCR), which provides a quantitative readout of allelic expression (Supplementary Fig. 13c). E105 inhibition signiﬁcantly reduced the maternal-to-paternal expression ratio of Copg2 (Fig. 5d), corresponding to a decrease in the maternal fraction from 67% to 57% (Supplementary Fig. 13d). Relative to a biallelic baseline of 50% maternal expression, this represents a loss of ~60% of the neuron-speciﬁc maternal bias. Notably, E105 is not the closest element to either promoter, indicating that its regulatory effects are not explained by linear proximity. The E105 region exhibits histone modiﬁcations characteristic of active enhancers, including H3K4me1 and H3K27ac, across mouse brain and other tissues (Fig. 5e, and Supplementary Fig. 13e). CRISPRimediated repression of E105 resulted in a signiﬁcant, though incomplete, reduction of H3K27ac at the enhancer site in NPC-derived neurons (padj = 1.7 × 10−13; Fig. 5e), without affecting H3K27ac at the Mest or Copg2 promoters (padj > 0.95; Supplementary Fig. 13f–h). These results indicate that partial repression of E105 is sufﬁcient to alter imprinted expression at this locus. Transcriptome-wide analysis conﬁrmed that E105 functions as a selective regulatory element. Total RNA-seq showed that E105 inhibition speciﬁcally reduced Mest expression with minimal effects on other genes, including total Copg2 levels (Fig. 5f). However, allele-speciﬁc analysis revealed a reduction in the Copg2 maternal-to-paternal expression ratio, while monoallelic Mest expression remained unchanged (Fig. 5f). To validate the role of E105 using an independent approach, we deleted E105 using dual gRNAs and catalytically active Cas9 in hybrid NPCs (Supplementary Fig. 13i, j). Despite heterogeneous editing outcomes, including ~33% of alleles with E105 deletion (Supplementary Fig. 13i,j), NPC-derived neurons recapitulated reduced Mest expression and reduced Copg2 allelic bias by RT-qPCR and RT-ddPCR analyzes (Fig. 5g). We further assessed in vivo relevance using AAV-mediated delivery of E105-targeting gRNAs into adult dCas9-KRAB mouse brain via retro-orbital injection. Approximately 45% of nuclei in the brain were transduced (Supplementary Fig. 13k), and cortical RT-qPCR analysis revealed a ~20% reduction in Mest expression relative to controls (Supplementary Fig. 13l). To assess CRISPRi efﬁciency in the NPC differentiation system used for the screen, we performed H3K9me3 CUT&Tag as a readout of dCas9-KRAB activity following gRNA transduction. Targeting of E104 and E105 successfully induced H3K9me3 at their respective loci, whereas E111 did not (Supplementary Fig. 13m), indicating variable gRNA efﬁciency. Thus, we cannot exclude the possibility that additional regulatory elements contribute to Mest-Copg2 regulation. Together, these results identify E105 as a distal enhancer that selectively regulates Mest expression and modulates allelic bias at Copg2 within this imprinted domain.

Discussion Our study reveals that allele-speciﬁc chromatin architecture is a common feature of imprinted domains in the mouse brain and is closely linked to the regulation of imprinted gene expression. Consistent with established models, we ﬁnd that DNA methylation-sensitive CTCF binding at ICRs is associated with allele-speciﬁc chromatin insulation. Loss of DNA methylation leads to biallelic CTCF binding, increased insulation at normally methylated alleles, and disruption of allelespeciﬁc chromatin organization, accompanied by reduced allelic expression bias. These ﬁndings provide systematic support for a model in which DNA methylation restricts CTCF binding and chromatin insulation to a single parental allele across imprinted domains. Beyond insulation at ICRs, our results indicate that allele-speciﬁc chromatin organization also modulates distal regulatory interactions. Active alleles of imprinted genes exhibit increased interaction frequency with distal regions, consistent with promoter hubness, whereas inactive alleles show reduced connectivity. For genes lacking promoter-associated DMRs, differences in contact frequency are less pronounced; instead, allele-speciﬁc expression is associated with preferential engagement with active enhancer states. Together, these ﬁndings suggest that allele-speciﬁc gene regulation can arise from both quantitative differences in chromatin contacts and qualitative differences in the regulatory potential of interacting regions. Through CRISPRi screening, we identify a distal enhancer (E105) within the Mest–Copg2 domain that selectively regulates Mest expression and modulates allelic bias of Copg2. Chromatin interaction analyzes show that E105 engages different promoters on the two parental alleles, contacting Mest on the paternal allele and Copg2 on the maternal allele, thereby enabling allele-speciﬁc enhancer-promoter communication. The architectural logic is similar to the well-established paradigm at the H19–Igf2 locus, where a methylation-sensitive ICR establishes a boundary that governs allele-speciﬁc enhancer access. However, our data also reveal a key distinction: whereas the H19–Igf2 ICR primarily functions as an insulator that blocks enhancer access on one allele, the Mest–Copg2 domain exhibits a more complex regulatory architecture. Here, the ICR not only contributes to insulation but also participates in allele-speciﬁc chromatin interactions that direct enhancer engagement with different target genes. This suggests that ICRs can play multiple roles in organizing allele-speciﬁc regulatory interactions beyond simple enhancer blocking. Our results further integrate enhancer activity with antisense transcription in controlling imprinted gene expression. We show that E105 promotes maternal Copg2 expression, whereas transcription of the paternal antisense transcript MestXL represses Copg2, likely through transcription interference. These two mechanisms act on opposite parental alleles and together shape the allelic expression pattern of Copg2. This dual regulatory logic provides a mechanistic

framework for understanding how imprinted genes lacking promoterassociated DMRs can achieve allele-speciﬁc expression through coordinated activation and repression. Around the time of this work, a preprint reported that Copg2 maternal expression bias is established independently of MestXL and instead reﬂects stage-speciﬁc regulation during neural differentiation, with MestXL required for maintenance rather than initiation44. That study further proposed the involvement of an upstream enhancer acting in an allele-speciﬁc manner to promote maternal Copg2 expression. Our ﬁndings are consistent with this framework and extend it by providing direct functional and structural evidence for such a mechanism. Speciﬁcally, we identify a distal enhancer (E105) and demonstrate that it regulates Mest and Copg2 through allelespeciﬁc chromatin interactions, thereby deﬁning how enhancer activity is partitioned between parental alleles and integrated with antisense transcription. In addition to CTCF-mediated insulation, we identify transcription-associated chromatin features as an alternative mechanism contributing to allele-speciﬁc chromatin organization. At the Meg3 locus, allele-speciﬁc chromatin organization is associated with transcription-linked chromatin signatures rather than canonical CTCF binding at the ICR, indicating that multiple mechanisms can generate allele-speciﬁc chromatin architectures across imprinted domains. Several limitations in our study should be considered. DNMTi treatment induces genome-wide DNA demethylation, making it difﬁ- cult to distinguish direct effects at ICRs from indirect consequences of broader epigenetic changes. In addition, incomplete demethylation in certain cell types and variable efﬁciency of CRISPRi targeting may limit the identiﬁcation of additional regulatory elements. Future studies using locus-speciﬁc perturbations and higher-resolution approaches will be important to further deﬁne the causal relationships between DNA methylation, chromatin architecture, and gene regulation. Together, our ﬁndings support a model in which allele-speciﬁc chromatin architecture integrates DNA methylation, chromatin insulation, enhancer activity, and antisense transcription to regulate imprinted gene expression. More broadly, these results highlight how multiple layers of chromatin organization cooperate to generate parent-of-origin gene regulation in the mammalian genome.

Capture Hi-C library preparation Dissected mouse cortices from reciprocal F1 hybrids (two BL6 x CAST and two CAST x BL6; 7–8 weeks old) were snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. Frozen tissues were pulverized in liquid nitrogen using a Cellcrusher device and resuspended in 5 mL PBS by gentle inversion. Samples were crosslinked in 2% formaldehyde by adding 500 μL TC buffer (50 mM HEPES, 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.5 mM EGTA, and 22% formaldehyde; Sigma-Aldrich #252549) and incubated at room temperature for 20 min. For adherent cells (mESCs, n = 3 per condition; primary cortical neurons from BL6 x CAST, n = 4), cells were washed twice with PBS, scraped into 5 mL PBS, and directly crosslinked to a ﬁnal concentration of 2% formaldehyde. Crosslinking was quenched by addition of 289 μL stop solution I for 5 min at room temperature. Samples were centrifuged at 2000 × g for 15 min at room temperature, and pellets were stored at −80 °C until use. Capture Hi-C libraries were prepared using the Arima Hi-C kit (Arima Genomics) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cell pellets were resuspended in 20 μL lysis buffer and incubated at 4 °C for 30 min. Chromatin was conditioned using SDS solution at 62 °C for 10 min and quenched with 20 μL stop solution II at 37 °C for 15 min. Digestion was performed with Arima restriction enzymes by incubation at 37 °C for 60 min, 65 °C for 20 min, and 25 °C for 10 min. Biotin end repair was carried out at room temperature for 45 min, followed

by proximity ligation at room temperature for 15 min. Crosslinks were reversed with proteinase K by incubation at 55 °C for 30 min, 68 °C overnight, and 25 °C for 10 min. Proximity-ligated DNA was puriﬁed using AMPure XP beads. Proximity-ligated DNA was fragmented in 100 μL elution buffer using a Covaris S220 (140 W, 10% duty factor, 200 cycles per burst, 55 s) to a target fragment size of ~400 bp. Double-sided size selection was performed using 0.6X and 0.25X AMPure XP beads. Biotin enrichment was performed using 300-400 ng size-selected DNA and 12.5 μL T1 Streptavidin beads in 200 μL binding buffer. Washes were performed according to the Arima protocol, in 200 μL wash buffer at 55 °C for 2 min each and then 100 μL elution buffer. Washed beads were resuspended in 50 μL of water. End repair was then performed on bead-bound DNA by incubating in end repair mix at 20 °C for 15 min, 72 °C for 15 min, followed by adaptor ligation at 20 °C for 30 min. Samples were cleaned up by magnetizing beads and washing in 200 μL wash buffer at 55 °C for 2 min and in 100 μL elution buffer. Washed beads were resuspended in 34 μL water and immediately used for library ampliﬁcation using Herculase II Fusion polymerase (98 °C for 2 min followed by 10 cycles of 98 °C for 30 sec, 60 °C for 30 sec, 72 °C for 1 min, and then 72 °C for 5 min). Different index primer combinations were used for each sample. The ampliﬁed library was puriﬁed using 1X AMPure XP beads. For target capture, 1.5 μg ampliﬁed Hi-C library was pre-cleared of residual biotin using 50 μL T1 Streptavidin beads in a 230 μL reaction. Approximately 1 μg of pre-cleared Hi-C library was resuspended in 14 μL water and was hybridized to custom capture probes designed to mm10 genome (Agilent Technologies; Supplementary Figs. 2–9 coordinates of capture probes track were lifted over to mm39) in a thermocycler (95 °C for 5 min, 65 °C for 10 min followed by 60 cycles of 65 °C for 1 min, 37 °C for 3 s) and puriﬁed using 50 μL T1 Streptavidin beads. After stringent washes (70 °C for 5 min, 6 times), captured libraries were ampliﬁed using Herculase II polymerase (98 °C for 2 min followed by 13 cycles of 98 °C for 30 s, 60 °C for 30 s, 72 °C for 1 min, and then 72 °C for 5 min). Final library puriﬁcation was performed using 1X AMPure XP beads, pooled equimolarly, and subjected to Illumina PE150 sequencing (Novogene).

The SNP-masked genome was digested at Arima restriction enzyme sites using HiCUP_digester48. Capture Hi-C FASTQ ﬁles were mapped using HiCUP (v0.8.0), and allele phasing was performed with SNPsplit (v0.6.0) using “hicup.bam” ﬁles as input. Reads assigned to the same parental genome (“hicup.G1_G1.bam” or “hicup.G2_G2.bam”) were converted to pre-Juicer format using hicup2juicer (v0.9.0) with --usemid and --digest options. Using a custom script, read pairs were ﬁltered to capture regions and required to have MAPQ > 30 at both ends. For each sample, maternal and paternal read counts were normalized by subsampling the deeper allele. To control for strain-of-origin effects, reads from reciprocal crosses were merged by parent-of-origin; speciﬁcally, G1_G1.medium ﬁles from BL6 × CAST samples were merged with G2_G2.medium ﬁles from CAST × BL6 samples, and vice versa. For comparisons across tissues or cell types, capture-region reads were further subsampled to equal depth. Medium ﬁles were converted to.hic format using Juicer pre tool (v1.22.01). Contact matrices were visualized in R (v4.4.1) using plotgardener (v1.10.2)49 or Juicebox (v1.11.08)50. Chromatin loops were identiﬁed with Juicer HICCUPS using VC_SQRT normalization7. Pile-up analysis was performed using Coolpuppy51. Virtual 4 C plots were generated by extracting one-dimensional contact proﬁles from Capture Hi-C data, using a 10 kb window

Chromatin state annotation and contact frequency analysis For chromatin contact frequency analysis, a 5 kb window centered on the TSS of each gene was deﬁned as the anchor, and all Capture Hi-C contacts originating from this anchor were included in the analysis. To focus on distal interactions, contacts within ±50 kb of the anchor were excluded. Based on the imprinted expression pattern of each gene, TSS-anchored contacts were classiﬁed as originating from the active (predominantly expressed) or inactive allele. For non-imprinted genes, contacts from each parental allele were analyzed. Contact frequencies are reported as the fraction of total contacts across both alleles. For analysis of chromatin states associated with distal Capture Hi- C interactions, chromatin states were ﬁrst deﬁned using ChromHMM52

by integrating allele-speciﬁc and non-allelic epigenome datasets from neuronal cells and tissues. The input features included allele-speciﬁc CTCF, H3K36me3, H3K27me3, H3K27ac, and H3K4me3 proﬁles, together with non-allelic H3K4me1 data. Public datasets were obtained from GEO and ENCODE, including allele-speciﬁc H3K27me3 from primary cortical neurons (GSE118399), allele-speciﬁc H3K27ac and H3K4me3 from mouse frontal cortex (GSE30199), and non-allelic H3K4me1 from E15.5 mouse forebrain (ENCODE). Allele-speciﬁc CTCF and H3K36me3 datasets were generated in this study from primary cortical neurons. ChromHMM models were trained on binarized input tracks to segment the genome into twelve chromatin states (java – jar ChromHMM.jar LearnModel --numstates 12 --assembly mm39). Each distal Capture Hi-C interaction was assigned to a chromatin state based on the state at its distal interacting locus. For each allele category (nonimprinted paternal, non-imprinted maternal, imprinted active, and imprinted inactive), the average number of interactions per TSS for each chromatin state was calculated and normalized to the genomic coverage of that state. The twelve states were grouped into functional categories by manual annotation as active enhancers (strong H3K4me1 and/or H3K27ac outside RefSeq exons), transcribed regions (strong H3K27ac or H3K36me3 overlapping RefSeq exons), repressive chromatin (strong H3K27me3), and quiescent states (no detectable histone modiﬁcation signal).

CUT&Tag library preparation CUT&Tag libraries were prepared using CUT&Tag-IT kit (Active Motif). Cells were gently washed with PBS, scraped into 1 mL PBS, and 600,000 cells were used per sample (n = 2 per condition). Cells were pelleted at 300 × g for 4 min, resuspended in lysis buffer (10 mM Tris pH 7.4, 10 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM spermidine, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mM EDTA, and 0.25% IGEPAL CA-630), and incubated on ice for 5 min with gentle trituration. Nuclei were collected by centrifugation at 800 × g for 4 min, washed, and processed according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Nuclei were bound to conditioned concanavalin A beads and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against CTCF (Cell Signaling #2899), H3K36me3 (Active Motif #61902 Lot 23065105), H3K27ac (Active Motif #39136 Lot 28720002) or H3K9me3 (Active Motif #39062 Lot 24306101). After incubation with secondary

antibody for 1 h at room temp, beads were resuspended in diluted CUT&Tag transposomes in CUT&Tag Dig-300 buffer and incubated on an orbital rotator for 1 h at room temperature. After transposome binding, beads were washed three times with Dig-300 buffer. Tagmentation was induced by incubating beads in 125 μL of CUT&Tag tagmentation buffer for 1 h at 37 °C. washed with PBS, and dehydrated sequentially in 50%, 70%, and 100% ethanol. Fixed samples were stored at −20 °C until use. Samples were then equilibrated in ampliﬁcation buffer for 30 min at room temperature. Hairpin mixtures were prepared by snap-cooling in ampliﬁcation buffer and incubated with samples for 4.5 h at room temperature in a dark humidiﬁed chamber. After ampliﬁcation, excess ampliﬁers were removed by two 30 min washes in 5X SSCT followed by a 5 min wash. Nuclei were stained with Hoechst 33342 (1:2000 dilution; Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc #62249). Brain cryosection imaging Following isoﬂurane overdose, mice were perfused with PBS and then 4% PFA. Whole brains were dissected, ﬁxed overnight in 1% PFA at 4 °C, washed in PBS, and cryoprotected in 30% sucrose overnight at 4 °C. Brains were then incubated in a 1:1 mixture of OCT (Fisher Healthcare #23730571) and 30% sucrose for 30 min to 6 h, embedded in OCT, and stored at –80 °C. Cryosections were cut at 12–14 μm onto SuperFrost Plus slides (Fisher #1255015S24). For AAV-derived GFP imaging, nuclei were stained with Hoechst 33342 and mounted with ProLong Glass Antifade Mountant. Images were taken using a Zeiss Axio Scan Z1 with a 10X objective. The same procedure was applied to corresponding GFP images, and the proportion of GFPpositive nuclei relative to the total number of nuclei was calculated.
